title: PC141 Lab Syllabus (Fall 2026)
text:
The laboratory component of this course provides students with hands-on experience in
mechanics. Through structured experimental investigations, students develop a deeper
understanding of physical principles while strengthening experimental technique, data
analysis, uncertainty evaluation, and scientific communication skills.

title: PC141 Lab Syllabus (Fall 2026)
text:
By the end of the lab sequence, students will be able to:
• Set up and conduct experiments in mechanics.
• Collaborate effectively in small groups during investigations.
• Measure and report precision of analog and digital instruments.
• Identify and distinguish between systematic and random errors.
• Estimate, calculate, and interpret uncertainties in measurements and final results.
• Assess whether results agree within uncertainties.

title: PC141 Lab Syllabus (Fall 2026)
text:
1. Estimation, Order of Magnitude Calculations, and Bounding – Introduction to
measurement and estimation.
2. Repeating Measurements – Precision, accuracy, and repeatability in experiments.
3. Measuring “g” – Determining the acceleration due to gravity and examining air
resistance effects.
4. Coefficient of Friction – Measuring static and kinetic friction coefficients.
5. Torque and the Principle of Moments – Investigating torque, rotational equilibrium,
and balance.
6. Moment of Inertia / Lab Evaluation – Applying rotational dynamics to determine
inertia.

section: Requirements and Policies > Attendance and Makeup Policy
text:
Attendance at all registered laboratory sessions is mandatory.
If you will miss (or have missed) a lab session, email the instructor as soon as possible,
preferably before the scheduled session. All follow-up regarding missed labs will be
handled in person during your next lab or tutorial session.
Valid reasons for absence and required documentation include:
• Illness: documentation from a licensed medical professional or walk-in clinic
• Varsity athletics travel: official confirmation from Athletics
• Other circumstances: appropriate supporting documentation
Approved make-up labs must be arranged within one week, subject to section capacity and
laboratory safety constraints.
Please do not send sensitive medical information by email. Bring required documentation
with you to your next lab or tutorial session.
Unexcused absences will result in a grade of zero for the missed laboratory.

title: PC141 Lab Syllabus (Fall 2026)
section: Requirements and Policies > Digital Devices & Participation Policy
text:
Laboratory sessions are device-free environments.
• The use of cell phones, laptops, tablets, smart watches, or any electronic devices is
not permitted during labs. All devices must be turned off and stored away.
• Students must bring a printed copy of the assigned lab manual, a calculator, and a
lab notebook. Lab manual for the lab is posted 6-days before the lab day.
Students who do not bring a printed lab manual (or required materials) will receive a
participation grade of -10 for that lab, resulting in a 10% deduction from the total
mark for that specific lab session. The lab manual is posted well in advance, and
printing or access issues (e.g., printer failure, last-minute printing, location
constraints) do not constitute a valid excuse.
•
Alternate arrangements will be made in case of illness, holidays, or unforeseen disruptions.

title: PC141 Lab Announcements (MyLS)
section: Post lab 1 > Estimate the Olympic swimming pool problem
text:
An Olympic swimming pool is roughly 50.01m long and 31.45m wide.
How long will it take to fill such a pool with an ordinary garden hose?
Hint:
You need to make a reasonable estimate for the depth of the pool as you did in the lab for
the IAs height and explain how you came up with the estimate. Estimate the flow rate for
the garden hose in the same way. Do the necessary calculations and explain your result.
Postlabs: Post lab Question (PQ) and IQ4 and IT4 are due by one week.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This post lab submission is due by one week at midnight after the lab session:
i.e. if your upcoming lab is on Thursday, October 14 at 2:30pm; your post lab must be
submitted by Thursday, October 21 at midnight.
You should submit an electronic version of the post-lab question through the Dropbox of
MyLS, Lab1 folder.

title: PC141 Tutorial Announcements (MyLS)
text:
The tutorial component is held every week and is designed to support students in
developing strong conceptual understanding, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills
in physics.
Tutorials provide a structured and supportive environment in which students actively
engage with physics problems related to the course material. Each session focuses on
reasoning, application, and analysis, rather than passive review.
During tutorials, we work through carefully selected problems together. Students receive
real-time guidance and feedback, encouraging them to:
• Think critically about physical situations in a variety of contexts
• Apply physics concepts with increasing confidence
• Refine the accuracy, clarity, and coherence of the reasoning
This iterative, hands-on problem-solving process strengthens conceptual foundations and
cultivates a methodical scientific mindset—skills essential for success in both academic
studies and professional scientific or technical fields.

the course.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
In this lab we will begin to build the foundation for working withmeasurement
uncertainty. Before learning formal methods, it is essential to practice concepts
such asestimation,bounding, andorder-of-magnitude reasoning. Especially when it is
useful in situations where quantities cannot be measured directly. These skills help us
decide whether a result is reasonable and how reliable it might be.
These skills form the first step toward a systematic treatment of uncertainty, which
you will develop further in later labs. These first steps mirror how scientists approach
real problems: starting with rough estimates, bounding possibilities, and then refining
to quantified uncertainties.

text:
Although science is rooted in precise measurement, scientists and engineers often begin
with approximate estimates. These serve as a ‘sanity check’—a way to anticipate
results, choose appropriate instruments, and identify mistakes early (e.g., wrong units
or unrealistic values). This exercise about how to move confidently between rough
intuition and systematic measurement.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
In many experiments, you will face situations where quantities cannot be measured
immediately or directly. In these cases, it is valuable to begin with anestimate—a
reasoned approximation of the result you expect. Estimation helps you decide what
instruments or methods are appropriate and provides a reference point against which
later measurements can be compared.
What matters most is not whether your estimate is exact, but whether you have a
clear idea of how far off itcouldbe. Even a rough estimate can be very useful when it
helps you detect mistakes, choose equipment, or check the plausibility of results.
Mini rule-of-thumb:Estimates within a factor of 2–3 are typical of reasonable
human judgment. A difference of a full order of magnitude (a factor of 10) often
signals a unit error or faulty reasoning.

A natural companion to estimation isbounding. Bounding a quantity means identi-
fying values that itcannotreasonably exceed or fall below. Anupper boundis a
value greater than the true result, while alower boundis a value smaller than the
true result. Together, these bounds form a safe “bracket” around the unknown value.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.2 Bounding > 3.2.1 Picking Realistic Bounds
text:
Reasonable bounds can often be set by comparison with known quantities. For
example:
• To estimate a person’s height, you might compare them with friends or family
members of known height. A taller person gives an upper bound; a shorter
person gives a lower bound.
• To estimate the mass of an unfamiliar object, you can compare it to objects you
know well. Something clearly heavier provides an upper bound, while something
lighter provides a lower bound. Wide bounds are safe but not useful. Narrower
bounds make your estimate more powerful.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
When the unknown quantity is similar to something you already know, comparison is
one of the most effective tools for estimation. If you can bracket the unknown value
between a higher and a lower bound, you can usually place your estimate somewhere
in between with reasonable confidence.
For example, if you know the mass of one object is smaller than your upper bound
and larger than your lower bound, then your estimate should reflect a value between
those two reference points.

section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.4 Less Familiar Comparison
text:
In some cases, it is not easy to find a familiar object to compare with the quantity of
interest. When there is nothing clearly similar, your estimate will naturally become
less precise and the bounds you choose will be more uncertain.

Tower. Unlike comparing a person’s height to family or friends, there is no everyday
reference object that is truly comparable. In such situations, estimates and bounds
must be broader and more approximate, yet they are still useful.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations
text:
In physics labs,order of magnitude (OM)calculations are often done early, using
preliminary or estimated data, to check whether results seem reasonable. They serve
Figure 1: Conrad Hall, for comparison
as a quick “sanity check” before spending time on precise measurements.
Order of magnitude refers to thepower of tenthat best describes a quantity. Raising
a number by one order of magnitude multiplies it by 10; lowering it divides it by 10.
For example:
•200 and 600 are the same order of magnitude (hundreds, or102).
•0.02 is one order of magnitude smaller than 0.2.
• A city with 1,000,000 people (106) is three orders of magnitude larger than a
town of 1,000 people (103).
Since an order of magnitude calculation is intended to be “within a factor of ten,” you
should be reasonably confident that:
•Ten times your value is clearly too large,
•One-tenth of your value is clearly too small.

Why Order of Magnitude Matters
• Error detection:Using the wrong unit (e.g., cm instead of m) will often shift
your result by several orders of magnitude, making the mistake obvious.
• Quick checks:Scientists use OM reasoning to judge whether a result is
physically realistic.
• Decision making:OM estimates guide choices of instrument sensitivity or
experimental method.

In physics labs,order of magnitude (OM)calculations are often done early, using
preliminary or estimated data, to check whether results seem reasonable. They serve
Figure 1: Conrad Hall, for comparison
as a quick “sanity check” before spending time on precise measurements.
Order of magnitude refers to thepower of tenthat best describes a quantity. Raising
a number by one order of magnitude multiplies it by 10; lowering it divides it by 10.
For example:
•200 and 600 are the same order of magnitude (hundreds, or102).
•0.02 is one order of magnitude smaller than 0.2.
• A city with 1,000,000 people (106) is three orders of magnitude larger than a
town of 1,000 people (103).
Since an order of magnitude calculation is intended to be “within a factor of ten,” you
should be reasonably confident that:
•Ten times your value is clearly too large,
•One-tenth of your value is clearly too small.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations > 3.5.1 Example: How many gold parking spaces are there at Laurier?
text:
Estimation problems in science often ask us to reason from limited data. The goal is
not to get an exact number but to reach a reasonableorder-of-magnitudeestimate.
Let us try this with the number ofgold parking spaces(faculty and staff only) on
campus.
1. Gold lots are reserved for faculty and staff, so the number of spots must be
smaller than the total number of employees at Laurier, since many walk, take
the bus, or carpool.
2. There are several lots of different sizes. A good strategy is to estimate the
average size of a lot and multiply by the number of lots.
From observation:
• The lot in front of the Science Building has about 50 spaces (roughly 25 per
side).
•Suppose there are about 10 similar lots across campus.
IfSis the average number of spaces per lot andLis the number of lots, then
N=S×L
so withS≈50andL≈10,
N≈50×10 = 500.
Does this make sense?
•More than 50?Yes—since one lot already has about 50.
• Less than 5000?Laurier has about 10,000 students. For 5000 gold spots to exist,
there would need to be one faculty or staff member for every two students. In
reality, the ratio is closer to 1 staff for every 10 students, so 5000 is much too
high.
Thus, an estimate of about500 gold spotsis reasonable.
One of the important features of order-of-magnitude reasoning is that it is often
self-correcting: you may overestimate some parts and underestimate others, but the
errors tend to balance out, leaving you close to the right order of magnitude.

text:
Any time you use anestimatedquantity in a calculation, you are performing anorder
of magnitude (OM) calculation. The purpose is not to obtain an exact answer,
but to check whether the result falls in a reasonable range.
Theorder of magnitudeof a quantity refers to the power of ten that best describes it.
For example:
• The height of a typical building might be written as∼ 101 metres (tens of
metres).
•The length of an entire campus might be∼102 metres (hundreds of metres).
Thus, saying that the length of the Science Building is
•“about 100 metres,” or
•“between 50 and 200 metres,”
are both acceptable order-of-magnitude estimates. What matters is that the result
lands in the correctballpark.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: 3 Theory and Procedure > 3.5 Order of Magnitude Calculations > 3.5.3 When are Order of Magnitude Calculations used?
text:
Order of magnitude reasoning is common in science and engineering:
• Before experiments:to anticipate what range of values to expect, and to
decide which instruments or methods are suitable.
• During data collection:to check whether preliminary results make sense in
real time.
• Afterward:to identify errors, such as unit mistakes, which often shift results
by entire orders of magnitude.
Key idea:Any calculation involving at least one estimated quantity is an order-of-
magnitude calculation. The more estimates involved, the wider the range of possible
answers, but the result should still be close to the “real” answer. Errors often balance
out, making OM estimatesself-correcting.

Unlike a linear scale, where equal spacing means equal differences, a logarithmic scale

•from 0.1 to 1 is also one cycle.
Key idea:If two numbers fall within the same cycle of a logarithmic scale, they
are within one order of magnitude of each other. This is why logarithmic plots are
especially useful for comparing estimates.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
text:
Estimation and bounding naturally lead us to the idea ofuncertainty. An uncertainty
tells us how confident we are about a measured or estimated value, expressed as a
central value± some range. Instead of always writing separate lower and upper
bounds, we compress this information into a single statement.
From Bounds to UncertaintyIf you can state a credible lower boundL and
upper boundU, a practical estimate and uncertainty are:
ˆx= L+U2 ,∆x≈ 12(U−L),report asx= ˆx±∆x.
• Uncertainty= the range we expect, based on limits of measurement or
estimation.
• Error= the actual difference between a measured value and the true value
(unknown in most real experiments).
Even if your value equals a “known” reference, you must still report an uncertainty.
Because uncertainty reflects how the value was obtained, not how close it happens
to be.

symmetric. Here,Edenotes your best estimate of the quantity.
3. Record eachexperimental statementin the form x = ˆx±∆x with correct
units.
Notation
The uncertainty in a symbol is indicated with the Greek letter∆. If a mass ism, then
∆m denotes theuncertainty in the mass, and you would writem± ∆m. Uncertainties
are always reported aspositivenumbers.

text:
By the end of this exercise, you should understand the following terms and ideas:
• Estimate:a rough calculation of a quantity when direct measurement is not
possible.
•Bound:upper and lower limits that frame where a quantity is likely to fall.
•Range:the difference between the upper and lower bounds.
• Order of magnitude:the scale or power of ten that best describes the size of
a quantity.
• Logarithmic scale:a nonlinear scale used to represent values that span several
orders of magnitude.
• Uncertainty:the confidence interval around an estimate, expressed as± some
value.
• Agreement:when two values with uncertainties overlap in their ranges, sug-
gesting they may represent the same true value.

title: PC141 Lab Manual: Estimation and Bounding
section: Appendix A: Reference Material > A.1 Significant Figures (SigFigs)
text:
Why they matter.Significant figures reflect the precision of a measurement and
keep reported results consistent with the quality of the data.
Core rules
•All nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 123.4 has 4 sig figs).
•Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 1002 has 4 sig figs).
•Leading zeros arenotsignificant (e.g., 0.00450 has 3 sig figs).
• Trailing zeros are significantifa decimal point is present (e.g., 45.00 has 4 sig
figs; 4500 has 2 sig figs unless written as4.500×103).
Operations
• Multiplication/Division:keep the same number of sig figs as the factor with
the fewest sig figs.
Example:(2.6cm)×(3.14cm) = 8.164cm 2→8.16cm 2 (3 sig figs).
•Addition/Subtraction:round to the least precisedecimal place.
Example:12.30 + 0.456 = 12.756→12.76(hundredths place).
Worked exampleYou measure a block’s edges as12.3cm,3 .40cm, and0 .85cm.
Volume:
V= (12.3)(3.40)(0.85) = 35.511cm 3 →35.5cm 3
(3 sig figs overall; the limiting factor is 0.85 with 2 sig figs? No—0.85 hastwosig figs,
so strictly you should report35cm3. If your instrument actually supportsthreesig

Why they matter.Significant figures reflect the precision of a measurement and
keep reported results consistent with the quality of the data.
Core rules
•All nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 123.4 has 4 sig figs).
•Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 1002 has 4 sig figs).
•Leading zeros arenotsignificant (e.g., 0.00450 has 3 sig figs).
• Trailing zeros are significantifa decimal point is present (e.g., 45.00 has 4 sig
figs; 4500 has 2 sig figs unless written as4.500×103).
Operations
• Multiplication/Division:keep the same number of sig figs as the factor with
the fewest sig figs.
Example:(2.6cm)×(3.14cm) = 8.164cm 2→8.16cm 2 (3 sig figs).
•Addition/Subtraction:round to the least precisedecimal place.
Example:12.30 + 0.456 = 12.756→12.76(hundredths place).
Worked exampleYou measure a block’s edges as12.3cm,3 .40cm, and0 .85cm.
Volume:
V= (12.3)(3.40)(0.85) = 35.511cm 3 →35.5cm 3
(3 sig figs overall; the limiting factor is 0.85 with 2 sig figs? No—0.85 hastwosig figs,
so strictly you should report35cm3. If your instrument actually supportsthreesig
figs for each edge, keep 3 sig figs. Match this to your instrument’s markings.)

sig figs),4.50×10 3 (3), or4.500×10 3 (4).

title: Examinations
text:
The university shall conduct a final examination period in each academic session for undergraduate students. End of course evaluation methods may take a variety of forms, including oral presentations, take-home examinations, major assignments, remote synchronous assessments, and proctored examinations.
Examinations are randomly scheduled and students may be required to write final examinations at any time between 8:30am-10:00pm, regardless of the regularly scheduled hours of their course. The maximum time allowed for the writing of a formally scheduled final examination will be two and a half hours (150 minutes). Students must refrain from making any commitments (i.e. travel or vacations) during the examination period. Students are required to be available for examinations during the examination periods of all terms in which they register. Students who register in courses from in more than one academic term or at more than one academic institution are responsible for any examination conflicts generated by their actions.
Three exams in 24 hours

title: Examinations
text:
Students are not required to complete more than two final examinations in a 24 hour period. In order to receive relief under this rule, the third scheduled examination must start and finish within 24 hours of the beginning of the first examination. For example, students will not receive relief under this regulation when their examinations begin at, 9:00 am and 2:00 pm on one day, and 9:00 am on the following day. To receive relief under this regulation students must complete the Final Exam Conflict Form at least seven calendar before the final day of classes of the term. The university reserves the right to select which examination is rescheduled. Approved requests will have an exam scheduled to a different day and time within the examination period.
Requests after the deadline can be submitted as a deferred exam petition to the appropriate Petitions Committee. If approved by the Petitions Committee, the exam will be scheduled during the deferred exam period and a non-refundable deferred examination fee will be applied. The university reserves the right to select which examination is to be deferred.
Simultaneous Exams

title: Examinations
text:
Final examinations take place at the end of every term. Candidates are expected to fulfill this obligation in an honest manner.
As an academic institution, the university's credibility depends upon the integrity of the examination process. With this in mind, the following are a set of rules to guide candidates:
Attendance and Identification
• Candidates are responsible for arriving at the correct time and location. Forgetfulness or inadvertently arriving at the wrong time or place cannot be considered acceptable excuses.
• Candidates must sign in to the exam and show their Laurier student identification cards when requested.
Examination Process
• The doors of the examination room will be opened approximately 10 to 30 minutes before the start of the examination. Candidates will be permitted to enter the examination room quietly up to 30 (thirty) minutes after the scheduled start of the exam. Candidates arriving late will not be allowed any extra time.
• Candidates must not begin the examination or attempt to read the examination questions until instructed to do so.
• In no case may a candidate leave the room temporarily, for any reason, until 30 (thirty) minutes after the start of the examination. After 30 (thirty) minutes from the start of the examination, candidates may not leave the exam room before completing and submitting the exam unless accompanied by a Proctor.
• Candidates are not permitted to submit their examination until their attendance has been taken.

title: Examinations
text:
• Candidates are not permitted to submit their examination until one hour after the examination has begun.
• Candidates must remain seated and may not leave the examination room during the last 15 minutes of the examination session.
• When a candidate finishes their exam, they must submit their materials with their name and student ID on all components including:
- All completed and attempted work
- Notes made during the exam
- Their copy of the examination paper
- Their multiple choice form (if used)
- Any other exam materials
• If a candidate does not put their name and student ID on one or more components of the final exam, the instructor reserves the right to not grade that component and assign a grade of 0.
• Unused examination supplies (booklets, multiple choice forms, scrap paper, etc.) may not be taken from the examination room.
• At the close of the examination period, candidates must stop writing immediately. The Presiding Officer and proctors may seize the papers of candidates who fail to observe this requirement, and a penalty may be imposed at the discretion of the instructor.
• Talk or any form of communication between candidates is absolutely forbidden. No information of any kind is to be written for the purpose of assisting other candidates. Responses to questions must not be done in an exaggerated way or in a manner that will involve transmission of information to others.

title: Examinations
text:
• Candidates must remain seated during the examination period. A candidate needing to speak to the proctor (e.g., to ask for additional supplies or to request permission to leave the examination room for any reason) should so indicate by raising their hand.
• Questions concerning possible errors, ambiguities or omissions in the examination paper must be directed to the proctor who will investigate them through the proper channels. The proctor is not permitted to answer questions other than those concerning the examination process.
Materials and Aids
• Candidates must not use or attempt to use any unapproved source of information. No candidates for an examination may bring into the examination room any books, notes or other material containing information pertaining to the examination unless the examiner has given instructions that such material will be allowed and this instruction is specified on the examination paper.
• Before a candidate takes their seat, the Presiding Officer and Proctors will specify whether:
- Backpacks or other bags and carriers may be brought to the desk site and placed under the chair where the candidate is writing the examination, or placed in a designated area during the examination. All electronic devices are to be turned off, should they be stored in backpack or other bag or carrier.

title: Examinations
text:
Final examinations for any course cannot be deferred more than twice. Students may receive a maximum of five exam deferrals during the completion of their degree.
If for reasons of illness or an unavoidable conflict a student cannot write a final exam as scheduled, the following options are available:
• The student may apply to the instructor or designate to be allowed to write the exam at an alternative time, ideally during the regularly scheduled examination period, but at the latest not beyond the date by which final grades for the last scheduled exam are to be submitted to the Office of Enrolment Services (i.e., one week after the scheduled examination period ends). There is no charge for this application. The procedures for application, approval, and implementation of these 'in-house alternative' examinations shall be established at the departmental level.
• The student may apply to the instructor for aegrotat standing (refer to policy section on Aegrotat Standing which follows). There is no charge for this application.

section: Religious Accommodations and Final Examination Scheduling
text:
Students submit the “Student Request for Accommodation for Religious Observances” form to request a religious accommodation for a final examination. The form is automatically submitted to the relevant Petitions Committee.
The deadline to request a final examination deferral is 7 calendar days before the final day of classes of the term. Deferral requests received by the deadline will not be charged a deferred examination fee, and the exam will be scheduled by the Faculty that owns the course on a designated slip day. If a student is not available on the date of a Slip Day they must follow regulations to defer the Slip Day exam.
For deferral requests submitted after the deadline, if approved by the Petitions Committee, the exam will be scheduled during the deferred exam period and a non-refundable deferred examination fee will be applied.
Deferral requests on religious grounds do not count towards the maximum of 5 exam deferrals that are permitted.

If a student is not available on the date of a Slip Day they must follow regulations to defer the Slip Day exam.
For deferral requests submitted after the deadline, if approved by the Petitions Committee, the exam will be scheduled during the deferred exam period and a non-refundable deferred examination fee will be applied.
Deferral requests on religious grounds do not count towards the maximum of 5 exam deferrals that are permitted.

title: Examinations
section: Religious Accommodations and In-term Test/Midterm Exam Scheduling
text:
Students submit the Student Request for Accommodation for Religious Observances form for a religious
accommodation request for an in-term test/midterm exam.
The deadline to request a religious accommodation for an in-term test or midterm exam that is identified on the syllabus is:
12-week and full-year courses: Must be submitted on or before 14 days after the start of term.
6-week courses: Must be submitted on or before 7 days after the start of term.
If the requested absence occurs within the first two weeks of the start of term for 12-week or full-year courses, or within the first week of the start of the term for 6-week courses, or if the dates are not known well in advance, students need to alert the instructor as soon as scheduling conflicts arise by completing the Student Request for Accommodation for Religious Observances form, which should be submitted within one week of identification of such conflict.
Requests received by the deadline will be granted a deferred in-term test or midterm (or equivalent), to be scheduled and administered by the instructor or as per faculty procedures (if applicable). Re-allocating the weight of the in-term test or midterm to the final exam or an assessment(s) listed in the course syllabus is not an acceptable accommodation for requests received by the deadline.
For requests submitted after a deadline, the course instructor can choose to accommodate the request and re-allocating the weight to another course assessment is acceptable.

title: Examinations
text:
A validating examination is a special examination, which is required of a student requesting advanced standing in a course not beyond the 100 level. The course may have been completed at a post-secondary institution of less than university status, which in Canada or the United States is neither a member nor an affiliate of a member of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada or the American Association of Universities and Colleges. Such examinations must be completed within one year of the date of admission to Wilfrid Laurier University. A final examination may be used as a validating examination.
Students will not receive credit until they have completed a course at this university.
To write a validating examination, the student must make application to the Office of Enrolment Services as well as receive permission from the department concerned. A fee is charged and is not refundable. Students admitted to the Faculty of Music will be governed by the statement on Validating Examinations in the Faculty of Music chapter.

title: Examinations
text:
In exceptional circumstances, students may be eligible to be exempted from writing the final examination in a course. Students should apply to their instructor as soon as the relevant circumstances are known. This should be done before the examination time, after consulting the specific aegrotat policies and procedures in the particular faculty or department involved. Students are eligible to be considered for aegrotat standing only if (a) a special situation warrants it and (b) if a sufficient amount of required term work has been completed satisfactorily as determined by the faculty or department. title: Examinations
section: Virtual Campus Courses: In-Person Midterms, In-Person Assessments, and In-Person Final Examinations Policy
text:
This policy outlines where students are required to write in-person mid-terms, in-person assessments and in-person final examinations for virtual courses, based on their home campus designation and term registration. A virtual course includes the following delivery modes: virtual asynchronous, virtual synchronous, and virtual hybrid.
In-person mid-terms, assessments, and final examinations for virtual courses will be made available at every in-person campus where the course is available for registration and has students enrolled from that campus. This includes regularly scheduled in-person midterms, assessments and final examinations and any approved for an alternate time (including religious accommodations and deferred examinations).
If a campus is restricted from registering in the course, these in-person requirements will not be provided at that campus.
Students whose home campus is restricted from enrolling in the course but have received an override to enrol in the course must complete in-person mid-terms, assessments, and final examinations, and any approved for an alternate time, at a campus where enrollment is permitted.
Campus restrictions can be viewed in LORIS under the Class Details section, within the 'Restrictions' tab.
Students with a virtual home campus must follow the designated process outlined below to arrange in-person requirements.
All Students

title: Examinations
section: Virtual Campus Courses: In-Person Midterms, In-Person Assessments, and In-Person Final Examinations Policy
text:
Students enrolled in at least one on-campus course (including in-person, hyflex, or in-person hybrid modes) during a given term are required to write all in-person mid-terms, assessments and final examinations on campus at their home campus, including in-person exams of virtual courses. These students are not eligible to write in-person mid-terms, assessments or examinations off-campus under any circumstances.
All in-person mid-terms, assessments and examinations for a given term must be written at the same Laurier campus; switching campuses for individual mid-terms, assessments and examinations is not permitted.
On-Campus Students
Students whose home campus is Waterloo, Brantford, or Milton must write their in-person midterms, assessments and examinations at their designated home campus. Students who arrive at a campus other than their designated home campus may not be accommodated to write, as seating and materials are prepared only for students assigned to that location.
A student can find their home campus on the verification of enrolment form, which is available through LORIS.
Determining Student Location
Student location for the purposes of determining eligibility to write off campus is determined based on the home address listed in the student’s official records. Students will be required to provide proof of address upon request.
On-Campus Students Enrolled Exclusively in Virtual Courses

text:
In instances where an on-campus student is enrolled exclusively in virtual courses in a term, the following location regulations apply (for that term):

• One term (i.e. Fall, Winter, Spring) and full-year courses: Must be submitted on or before 14 calendar days after the start of term.
• 6-week courses: Must be submitted on or before 7 calendar days after the start of term.
• Students who are located more than a 150 km radius from any Laurier campus:
• Will be assigned to write at their home campus. If a student prefers to write at a different Laurier campus due to proximity, they must submit a request using the form available on the Proctored Exams webpage. The deadline to submit this request:
• One term (i.e. Fall, Winter, Spring) and full-year courses: Must be submitted on or before 14 calendar days after the start of term.

title: Grades
text:
A student's progress within a program will be evaluated on the basis of the cumulative grade point average (GPA) for all graded courses on the Laurier undergraduate academic record. For purposes of calculation, the grade point (GP) earned in a 0.5 credit will be given half the weight of that earned in a 1.0 credit. Likewise the GP earned in a 0.25 credit will be given a quarter of the weight of that earned in a 1.0 credit.
For example, a student with an A (11.0) in a 1.0 credit, a C- (2.0) in a 0.5 credit and a B+ (2.25) in a 0.25 credit will receive a GPA of 8.71. (15.25 grade points divided by 1.75 credits)
Where letter grades are derived from percentages, the following conversion will be adopted unless the instructor announces otherwise, in writing, at the outset of a course.
Letter grades and their grade point equivalents are as follows:
Letter Grades – Grade Points – Percentage Conversion
A+ – 12 – 90-100
A – 11 – 85-89
A- – 10 – 80-84
B+ – 9 – 77-79
B – 8 – 73-76
B- – 7 – 70-72
C+ – 6 – 67-69
C – 5 – 63-66
C- – 4 – 60-62
D+ – 3 – 57-59
D – 2 – 53-56
D- – 1 – 50-52
F – 0 – 0-49
XF * – 0 – 0-49
DR ** – 0 – 0-49
GNR – - – Grade not Reported
UR*** – - – Under Review
* Final exam or final assessment not written - failed course.
Where an X appears beside a final passing grade, the final examination was not written or final assessment not completed, and the grade is based upon term work with a 0 on the final exam or final assessment.

title: Grades
section: Calculation of Grade Point Average: Repeated Course
text: When a course is repeated the grade received in the second attempt will be used to calculate the GPA. Special averages (i.e., those calculated for distinctions) do not conform to this practice. Students in degree programs may repeat courses up to a maximum of 2.0 credits. When a course is repeated, the first attempt will remain on a student's transcript, and will not be used for credit toward the program.

It should be noted that an instructor may require a student to take the final examination in order to qualify for obtaining a passing grade in the course.

There are 4 sequential steps a student may take for a grade appeal. A student may choose not to proceed to a subsequent step at any point in the process. A student may submit only one (1) grade appeal per course section.

title: Grades
text:
Students who believe that the final grade received in a course does not reflect their academic performance should consult with the course instructor. The instructor may review components of the course, including the final examination with the student. A request for a final grade reassessment to the instructor may be submitted as soon as the final grade is posted to LORIS (unofficial record of coursework) but must be submitted no later than 10 business days after the start of the immediately following term or no later than 10 business days after the grade is posted (unofficial record of coursework), whichever is later. If necessary, the instructor can initiate a grade change through the grade change form.
Step 2: Chair
Note: In the event the course is part of an interdepartmental program, or as determined by faculty structure, the delegated authority and responsibilities of the chair may be represented by a Program Coordinator, Associate Dean, etc.
If the course instructor is unavailable (allow 5 business days for a response), or if the student remains dissatisfied after the instructor consultation, the student may request a final grade appeal to the chair (or delegate) of the department offering the course. The chair shall serve as arbiter. In the case where the chair or delegate is the instructor, the associate dean of the faculty shall assume the functions of the chair.

title: Grades
text:
The request shall be filed in writing and shall contain a statement of the specific grounds for the belief that the grade does not reflect the student's academic performance in the course and must be accompanied by the relevant course work, which has been returned to the student, and a summary with evidence of the outcome of the instructor consultation. It should not contain grounds or information that have not been presented to the instructor. Appeals that do not meet these requirements will be dismissed. The student may review the final examination in the department office to prepare the official request. The request to the chair for a final grade appeal shall be filed no later than 10 business days of the conclusion of Step 1.
Only course work that can be objectively re-evaluated is eligible for reassessment. This excludes (but is not limited to) presentations, performances, participation marks, and peer evaluations, as these cannot be reassessed in the same manner. If the grade appeal is specific to a group project, the entire group must agree to the grade appeal being submitted. The chair has the discretion to determine whether an assessment not included on the list above qualifies for objective re-evaluation.

title: Grades
text:
The chair will determine, based on the request, whether all or individual components of coursework will be re-evaluated. This decision is at the chair's discretion. The chair shall provide the student with a written decision, to the student’s WLU email account, regarding the request for the final grade appeal within 20 business days of receipt of the request, with Enrolment Services copied. The chair’s decision, whether it results in a higher grade, lower grade, or no change, will stand as the final grade. The chair’s decision cannot be reconsidered at Step 2.
Steps for the Chair
• When a student requests a grade appeal, all individually completed work that can be objectively reevaluated can be re-assessed. This excludes (but is not limited to) presentations, performances, participation marks, group work and peer evaluations, as these cannot be reassessed in the same manner.
a. If a student requests an individual grade appeal, group projects are not re-evaluated.
b. If all members of a group request a grade appeal, the group project should be reevaluated, and any determined grade revision applies to all members of the group.

text:
• If the chair determines that the request lacks grounds for a final grade appeal due to the nature of the appeal being based on course policy, course structure, work that cannot objectively be reassessed, or personal circumstances affecting academic performance, or if it is missing information required for a grade appeal, the appeal will not be considered.

a. Confirmation that the Step 1 took place and its outcome.
b. All components or individual components of graded course materials, including feedback.
• The chair will identify a faculty member in the same department/program with disciplinary expertise and will request that they review the student’s work.
• The chair should not review the student’s work, as they are the arbiter of the process. If the chair is best suited to review the work due to disciplinary expertise, the associate dean will assume the role of arbiter.
• The faculty member will review the student’s work and assign grades and provide the grades to the chair.
• The chair will review the faculty member’s grades.
• The grade assigned by the faculty member, whether higher, lower, or the same, will stand.

title: Grades
text:
• The chair will notify the course instructor of the outcome and will provide the reassessed grades to the associate dean to be submitted for a final grade revision. The grade appeal decision, whether higher, lower, or unchanged, will stand as the final grade.
• The chair will notify the student of the outcome of the final grade appeal to the student’s Laurier email account, with Enrolment Services copied.
Step 3: Petitions Committee
The student may, following the release of the chair's decision, submit a petition to the faculty offering the course, the procedure for which is found in this chapter under Academic Regulations: Petitions. The petition must be submitted no later than 10 business days of the receipt of the chair’s decision (Step 2). The petition should not contain any grounds or information that have not been presented to the chair. The grade appeal fee will be applied to the student’s account if the faculty petitions committee denies the petition.
Step 4: Senate Student Appeals Committee
If a student wishes to appeal the decision of the Faculty Petitions Committee to the Senate Student Appeals Committee, they must submit their appeal within 10 business days of receiving the decision from the Faculty Petitions Committee. If the Senate Student Appeals Committee rules in the student’s favor, the grade appeal fee applied by the Petitions Committee will be refunded. If the appeal is denied, an additional grade appeal fee will be applied to the student’s account.

title: Adding and Dropping Courses
text:
Adding Courses:
• 12-week Terms: A course must be added no later than 10 business days from the beginning of term. This regulation applies to spring term, fall term, and winter term (12-week terms).
• 6-week Terms: A course must be added no later than 5 business days from the beginning of the term. This regulation applies to Intersession, Summer Session, Fall 6-week (first) and Winter 6-week (first).
• Fall 6-week (second): A course must be added no later than three business days before November 1.
• Winter 6-week (second): A course must be added no later than three business days before February 1.
Students should consult the Academic Dates to view the actual dates.
Courses may not be added after the specified deadline date. In exceptional cases a Petitions Committee may grant a petition to waive the regulation.
Consult the Academic Petitions website for more information. Students may add courses and using LORIS. Students should ensure that a course add has been completed by checking their academic record on LORIS. Courses adds that cannot be completed using LORIS can be submitted to Enrolment Services, through the Service Laurier website.

title: Adding and Dropping Courses
text:
All courses can by dropped through LORIS. Students should confirm that a course drop has been processed by checking their academic record on LORIS. If LORIS does now allow a course drop, students may submit a Drop Course Request Form to Enrolment Services (available on the Enrolment Services website). All course drops are subject to university regulations and published deadlines. The onus of dropping a course rests solely upon the student. Ceasing to attend lectures, even if the instructor is informed, does not formally constitute a dropped course and will result in a failing grade.
The final dates to drop a course(s) for possible tuition adjustment (assessed at course rate) are:
Fall term (12-weeks) – two-thirds of course, 40th teaching day
Winter term (12-weeks) – two-thirds of course, 40th teaching day
Fall and Winter (6-weeks, first and second) – two-thirds of course, 20th teaching day
Intersession, Summer Session (6-weeks) – two-thirds of course, 20th teaching day
Spring term (12-weeks) – two-thirds of course, 40th teaching day
Courses of different durations will be pro-rated.
Consult the Academic Dates for the actual dates to drop a course(s) for possible tuition adjustment (assessed at course rate). If the normal deadline date falls on a Friday, the actual deadline will become the following business day.
Final day to Drop a Course without Failure:

title: Adding and Dropping Courses
text:
The final day to drop a course(s) without failure is the last day of class of the term, identified in the academic dates as the “Classes End” date. Students remain responsible for 100% tuition for courses dropped after final day to drop for possible tuition adjustment (assessed at course rate) until 11:59 pm EST on the final day to drop a course without failure. After the final day to drop a course without failure, courses may not be dropped. In exceptional cases, a Petitions Committee may grant a petition to waive the regulation. Consult the Academic Petitions website for more information.
Dropping a Course After the Deadline (Grade of DR): A student may request to drop a course after the final day to drop a course without failure, but before the start of the exam period. A grade of DR (dropped-failure) will be assigned to the course(s) requested. To make this request, a student may email Enrolment Services (through the Service Laurier website) with the course code and section, and indicate that they accept the grade of DR.
Request to Change Course Registration to Audit:
A change from registration for credit to audit must be made no later than the final day to drop for possible tuition adjustment. This request can be made by completing the Audit Course Form on the Enrolment Services website. The Faculty teaching or department of the course must provide permission for a student to audit a course.

title: Faculty Petitions
text:
Petition Types
A student may appeal to the appropriate faculty petitions committee any decision made by an individual or body acting in the name of the university, which affects the academic standing of the student, and which the student believes was made without following due process and/or without full knowledge/evidence of extenuating circumstances.
Filing a Petition
Students must submit a petition to the Faculty in which they are/were registered during the term(s) identified in the petition in accordance with the established procedures for petitions, available on the Academic Petitions and Appeals website. . Exceptions to this process include course-specific petitions (e.g. deferred examination, petitions for an extension to course work, and petitions for a third attempt in a course). These petitions must be submitted to the faculty offering the course.
All petitions shall be commenced by filing the appropriate petition form, within twenty-five (25) working days of the onset of the issue or within twenty-five (25) working days of the decision being appealed. Petitions relating to academic misconduct must be filed no later than ten (10) working days of receiving the Final Notice of Penalty document. Refer to Procedures for Student Code of Conduct: Academic Misconduct for further information.

title: Faculty Petitions
text:
A Faculty Petitions Committee may waive submission deadlines at its discretion in special circumstances, provided the student submits supporting rationale and documentation specifically demonstrating the reasons why the deadline could not be met. The petition form includes a section for students to explain their reasons for missing the submission deadline and provide supporting documentation. If the late request is approved, the petitions committee will proceed to review the petition. If the late request is denied, the process ends, and the petition will not be considered.
As the student will not be able to appear in person before the petitions committee, it is important that the student ensure that all relevant materials, including a written detailed synopsis of the circumstances pertaining to the appeal and supporting documentation (if applicable) is submitted as part of the petition.
With the exception of the regulations pertaining to Grade Appeals, no petition or appeal may be commenced where the student has graduated from the program to which the petition or appeal relates.
Petition Committee Decisions
A petition will be decided on and the decision will be communicated to the student within thirty (30) working days of their petition submission, provided all documentation and information required from the student are submitted with the petition.

text:

The Petitions Committee may delegate decision-making authority to an appropriate academic or administrative representative, provided that the decisions are made in accordance with guidelines established by the committee. The petition decision letter provided to the student must indicate if the decision was made by a delegated authority.
The Petitions Committee and delegated authority reserves the right to make a different decision from what the student has requested if it determines that an alternative decision is more appropriate based on the circumstances and supporting documentation. In such cases, the alternative decision will be outlined in the decision letter sent to the student. The student will then have the option to accept or decline the alternative decision by a deadline provided in the decision letter.

title: Faculty Petitions
text:
A decision of an individual who was delegated decision-making authority by the faculty petitions committee may be appealed to the petitions committee. To appeal a delegated decision to the faculty petitions committee, students must include evidence that a procedural error was made in the delegated decision and/or that the delegated decision was made without full understanding and evidence of the extenuating circumstances. To initiate an appeal of a delegated decision, please contact the faculty petitions committee that made the original decision for information about the delegated decision appeal process.
A decision of a faculty petitions committee may be appealed by the student to the Senate Student Appeals Committee, in accordance with the Procedures for Considering Appeals.
A first offence of academic misconduct may not be appealed to the Senate Student Appeals Committee; the decision of the petitions committee is final.

text:
Students who register at Wilfrid Laurier University are subject to, and must become familiar with, the university's rules, regulations and policies and the university will assume that the student has done so.
The requirements in this calendar are official rules, regulations and policies of the university. Further rules applicable to students may be found in the sections entitled Student Code of Conduct and Discipline and the University Policies website.
The university will not be liable for any loss, damages or other expenses that the cancelling of programs or courses might cause.

title: Student Regulations
text:
There are occasions when students fall ill and are unable to attend classes, write scheduled tests or meet the deadlines for mid-term assignments. Faculty members may offer, at their discretion and without proof of a medical excuse slip, alternate arrangements so that students are able to satisfy the requirements of a course. In the event that a faculty member requests a medical excuse slip, students must comply with one of the following:
• A student must be examined by a member of the WLU Health Services staff at the time of the illness; the decision to issue a medical excuse slip and the dates for which the excuse slip are valid will be made by the examining doctor or nurse.
• A student must be examined by a qualified off-campus physician at the time of the illness; the decision to issue a medical excuse slip and the dates for which the excuse slip are valid will be made by the examining doctor who must be informed of the reason for the request.

title: Academic Misconduct Defined
text:
Academic misconduct, the term used for when individuals do not act with integrity in an academic setting, is defined in the Student Code of Conduct and Discipline.
Academic misconduct is an act by a student, or by students working on a team project, which may result in a false evaluation of the student(s), or which represents an attempt to unfairly gain an academic advantage, where the student either knew or ought reasonably to have known that it was misconduct. Whether or not a student intended to commit academic misconduct is not relevant for a finding of academic misconduct. Hurried or careless submission of assignments does not excuse students from responsibility for verifying the academic integrity of their work before submitting it.
Academic misconduct includes (but is not limited to):
• Plagiarism.
• Cheating.
• Submitting the same piece of work for more than one course without the instructor’s permission.
• Impersonating another person in a test or exam.
• Unauthorized collaboration on individual assignments, tests or exams.
• Buying or otherwise obtaining term papers or assignments.
• Falsifying, misrepresenting, or forging an academic record or supporting document.
These pages provide helpful information and resources to help you understand what academic misconduct is and how you can avoid it.

title: Academic Misconduct Defined
text: This involves using the thoughts, ideas, or writings of another person and passing them off as your own (adapted from the Oxford English Dictionary definition). It can involve taking credit for ideas that were not your own or using the words of others without properly citing them.

title: Academic Misconduct Defined

title: Academic Misconduct Defined
text: Self-plagiarism is submitting the same piece of work for more than one course without the instructor’s permission. You are not allowed to receive course credit for the same work twice. This means that you can’t use an essay from a course you took last year in one of your current courses, even if the topic is the same.

title: Academic Misconduct Defined
section: Types of Academic Misconduct > Unauthorized Collaboration
text: Sometimes your instructors will require you work with others in the class (e.g., a group project) and sometimes they will want you to work on your own (e.g., for a take-home exam). When you work with others (for example, on an assignment) when the instructor expects you to work on your own, it is considered to be unauthorized collaboration. Different instructors have different expectations and it’s your responsibility to find out if you are allowed to work with others or if you are expected to complete the work on your own.

title: Academic Misconduct Defined
section: Types of Academic Misconduct > Use of Unauthorized Aids During a Test or Exam
text: Unauthorized aids include anything that has not been cleared with your instructors as being allowed during the exam. You are allowed to have only the items that you will need to write the exam with you at your desk, and all your other belongings will need to be placed at the front of the room (including your phone and computer). If you are caught using any type of unauthorized aid (whether it’s a cheat sheet or a smart watch) it is considered cheating. Before writing your exams, you should be familiar with the university regulations for final exams.

title: Academic Misconduct Procedures
text:
There is a formal process for investigating cases of academic misconduct. This process is outlined in the Student Code of Conduct: Academic Misconduct.
If your instructor has a reasonable suspicion that you may have engaged in academic misconduct, here’s a summary of what you can expect if this is your first offence. (For the full policy and procedures and information about the process for second offences, please consult the policy and procedures).

Academic Misconduct Procedures | Overview
There is a formal process for investigating cases of academic misconduct. This process is outlined in the Student Code of Conduct: Academic Misconduct.
If your instructor has a reasonable suspicion that you may have engaged in academic misconduct, here’s a summary of what you can expect if this is your first offence. (For the full policy and procedures and information about the process for second offences, please consult the policy and procedures).

title: Academic Misconduct Procedures
text:
• The instructor will send you a form describing their concerns and inviting you to respond. Either you or the instructor can request a meeting to discuss the incident, or you can choose to respond in writing. In a meeting or your written response, you can ask questions, request clarification, and present your case. You may bring a support person to the meeting for assistance. You will have five working days (8:30 a.m. – 4:30 p.m., Mon – Fri) to request a meeting or respond in writing if you choose. Note that you are not required to request a meeting or provide a written response.
• After the five-day response period, the instructor will decide whether to proceed with an official allegation. If they elect to proceed, they will complete a formal allegation form explaining the details of their concerns and how you responded to the notification. The instructor will send the allegation to the relevant administrator (department chair or the associate dean, depending on your program) and will include you in the email. You then have five working days to request a meeting with or provide a written response to the relevant administrator if you choose to do so. The relevant administrator will confirm if you have any prior incidents of academic misconduct, will assess the allegation, and if they determine that academic misconduct has occurred, they will determine the penalty.
• If the relevant administrator determines that academic misconduct occurred, they will send you a document explaining the penalty.
First offences can be appealed by filing a petition by the deadline outlined in the procedures.

title: Gen AI Student Resource Hub
section: What is Generative AI? > Before You Use Gen AI, Ask Yourself Why
text:
One of the benefits of gen AI is speed. It can create content in seconds.
But university isn't just about completing tasks. It's also about developing knowledge, skills, and a way of thinking.
The time and effort devoted to learning – the learning struggle – is a good thing.
Before using gen AI, ask yourself: Am I learning, or am I skipping the learning?
Remember:
• If a task feels too hard: You are building new skills. Learning often feels challenging before it feels doable.
• If a task feels too time-consuming: Meaningful learning takes time. Quick answers don't always lead to lasting understanding.
• If a task feels too tedious: Consider what skills your instructor wants you to practice. The process may be just as important as the final result.
Gen AI can support learning, but it shouldn't replace the thinking, practice, and reflection that help you grow.
If you want to discuss how gen AI tools can be used to support and complement your academic skill-building and learning, book an appointment or attend a workshop with the Student Success team.

title: Gen AI Student Resource Hub
section: Can Gen AI Help Me? > Know the Risks
text:
Gen AI may be useful, but it can also be wrong. Before relying on any output, check the list below:
Did you know gen AI:
• Can sound confident while providing incorrect information or misinterpret information?
• Can invent sources or exaggerate facts?
• Can misinterpret complex questions and articles?
• Can reinforce biases and stereotypes?
• Cannot accurately perform numerical computations since its training data doesn't allow for numerical computations?
• Does not automatically use diagrams or graphs for quantitative explanations?
• Can give you a false sense of knowledge and understanding?

title: Gen AI Student Resource Hub
text:
If you’ve ever tried using Microsoft Copilot and been frustrated with the output, that may be because the prompt was weak. The quality of your results depends on the quality of your prompts.
The next time you write a gen AI prompt, include these elements:
• Task: What do you want the tool to do?
• Context: What background information is important?
• Examples: What other content is similar to what you are looking for?
• Persona: Should the AI respond as a tutor, editor, coach, professor, etc.?
• Format and Tone: How do you want the output presented (e.g., bullet points, formal tone, concise summary)?
Weak prompt: "Explain photosynthesis."
Better prompt: "Think like a Biology instructor and break down the different major ground tissues of plant bodies into multiple-choice quiz questions so I can quiz myself. Please include the characteristics of parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma. Don’t provide the answer as I want to ensure that it reflects my course content. Let’s start with five multiple-choice questions with four answer options."
*Adapted from the University of Saskatchewan, "Understanding Generative AI Series: Crafting Better Prompts." April 20, 2026.

title: Gen AI Student Resource Hub
section: Write Better Prompts > Evaluating Gen AI Outputs
text:
Not every gen AI output is accurate, reliable, and relevant. So, before using any outputs, apply the E.V.E.R.Y. framework.
• E – Evaluate: Does the output answer your question and do what you want it to do?
• V – Verify: Check the facts, sources, and claims made in the output.
• E – Engage: Ask follow-up questions to improve the gen AI response.
• R – Revise: Adapt the content to fit your specific context, style and tone. The output should be a draft, not your finished product.
• Y – You: Remember that you are responsible for everything you submit.
*Adapted from AI for Education, "How to Use AI Responsibly EVERY Time." August 31, 2026.

title: Deferred Exams
text:
Deferred examinations may be granted in limited circumstances and for legitimate reasons only, such as:
• Illness.
• Religious reasons (see Accommodations for Religious Observances).
• Extraordinary personal or family circumstances (e.g. death in the family).
• Scheduling conflict with another exam or 3 exams within 24 hours.
To be considered for deferred exam privileges, students must submit a petition as described below.
The following are not considered legitimate reasons for requesting a deferred exam:
• Appealing for more study time.
• Travel arrangements or vacation plans during the final exam period.
• Commuting.
Students must be available for exams during the examination periods of all terms in which they are registered and are responsible for ensuring they attend their final exams as scheduled.

title: Deferred Exams
text:
Final exams are a mandatory part of most courses. Students are expected to write the final exam for a course as scheduled by the Examinations Office. The majority of students complete a degree without ever deferring a final exam.
For information regarding deferring a final exam due to religious observance, see Accommodations for Religious Observances.
If you are unavailable to write the exam at the scheduled time due to extenuating circumstances or if you miss a final exam for legitimate reasons, you must appeal for deferred examination privileges.
All appeals for deferred exams must be directed to the petitions committee in the faculty in which the course is offered rather than the one in which you are registered. If you are unsure which faculty offers a course, you can find this information in the Undergraduate Academic Calendar. Be sure to see if faculty offering the course in question has additional faculty-specific information on exam deferrals.
A final examination cannot be deferred more than twice for any course. Students may receive a maximum of five exam deferrals throughout their degree. Deferred examination petitions are not automatically approved; each petition is reviewed before a decision is made.

title: Deferred Exams
section: Deferred Final Exams > Three Exams Within 24 Hours
text:
Students are not normally required to complete more than two final examinations in a 24-hour period. In order to receive relief under this rule, the third problematic exam must finish within 24 hours of the beginning of the first. The university reserves the right to select which exam is to be deferred. The deadline to submit the form is at least 7 calendar days before the final day of classes of the term.
Submit a petition for a deferred exam through the Faculty responsible for the second course in the sequence.
Deferred exam requests of this type are exempt from the deferred examination fee and do not count toward a student’s maximum allowable deferred exams.

title: Deferred Exams
text:
In lieu of documentation, medical grounds deferred examination petitions require a personal attestation, which is available directly on the petition form. The attestation is accepted in lieu of documentation within the maximum of five deferred examinations permitted. Should a student petition to exceed five deferred examinations, medical documentation will be required for deferral requests based on medical grounds.
All second deferral requests (a request to defer a previously deferred exam) based on medical grounds require medical documentation, in addition to the personal attestation.
For unforeseen medical grounds, requests should be submitted as soon as possible and no later than three business days after the scheduled date of the examination.
If you are sick on the scheduled date of a final exam and unable to write, do not write the exam. If you choose to write it, your attempt will count.

text:
The examination schedule is published in advance of the examination period to allow sufficient time for students to arrange their work schedules accordingly. Every effort must be made to ensure availability to write an exam at the scheduled date and time. Requests for deferred examinations due to work commitments are normally not approved. Special consideration will be given to students enrolled in Public Safety programs including: Paramedicine, Policing, Public Safety, Criminology and Policing (online).

The letter must include contact information and verification from your supervisor confirming that you are required to be available at your workplace at the time of the scheduled final examination.

title: Deferred Exams
section: Deferred Final Exams > Petitions on Other Grounds > Academic Integrity
text:
Accurate and complete disclosure of relevant information, provided in or to support a petition submission, is a fundamental expectation of the petition process. Misleading information, including the omission of relevant facts or circumstances, that could influence the assessment of a petition is considered a serious matter and may be treated as academic misconduct.
All supporting documentation must be complete and authentic and is subject to verification. Submitting documentation that is intentionally cropped, has information obscured, or is otherwise modified is a serious academic offense because the original content cannot be fully assessed or authenticated. Any supporting documentation that is fabricated will be treated as academic misconduct.
Allegations of misconduct will result in immediate denial of your petition and may also be considered for further penalties.

title: Deferred Exams
section: Deferred Final Exams > Petitions on Other Grounds > Generative AI Tools & Deferred Examination Petition Submissions
text:
Students should refrain from using generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot in their petition submissions. Written content should be completed by the student in their own words, as this best helps the committee understand the petition and the solution being requested. Submissions should reflect the student's personal understanding of the circumstances and the grounds for the petition.
Use of generative AI results in submissions that are generic, inaccurate, too wordy, or inadequately address the specific issues warranting the petition.

title: Deferred Exams
section: Deferred Final Exams > Petitions on Other Grounds > What Happens if a Deferral is Granted?
text:
Most students will write deferred exams during the next regularly scheduled deferred exam period. Typically, this takes place in the last week of the month following the originally scheduled exam. For example, if you successfully petition to defer a fall term exam scheduled for December, you will write your exam in the last week of January unless otherwise instructed. A grade of "DEF" will be assigned until the examination is written. See the academic calendar for more details.
Students who require their final grade sooner to meet prerequisite, progression, or graduation requirements may, time permitting, be able to write a deferred exam during a faculty-designated period commonly referred to as a "slip day." Slip day exams are typically held during or soon after the regularly scheduled examination period.
A non-refundable deferred examination fee applies. The fee effective as of Sept. 1, 2026, is $74. This fee is subject to change without notice. Please note that deferrals on the grounds of religious observance may be exempt from the deferral fee.

title: Deferred Exams
section: Faculty-Specific Forms and Information > Faculty of Science
text:
If you do not complete all required sections of the Faculty of Science Final Examination Petition Form, your petition will be closed and you will need to re-submit the form to be considered for a deferred examination.
After your Petition is Submitted
The standard non-refundable deferred examination fee will be charged to your Laurier student account for each deferred examination.
If granted, the deferral will be scheduled for the next university-wide deferral period (last week of May, August, September or January). The Faculty of Science schedules one “Slip Day” period. This date is reserved for deferred examinations for students who have petitioned for religious accommodations by the regulation deadline (seven calendar days before the final day of classes of the term).
The time required to process the deferral petition will vary from two to twenty business days (or more depending on the number of petitions received). Do not submit a second petition form, or inquire as to the status of your petition, unless a minimum of 20 business days has passed since the form was submitted.
A letter with the deferral petition decision will be sent to the student’s MyLaurier email address. A student is expected to monitor their email account for the decision, or any other correspondence related to their petition submission.
Questions?

title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
text:
Starting university is an exciting journey, but unexpected challenges can sometimes make it difficult to stay on track academically. If you need to take time away, whether for health, personal, financial, or academic reasons, you are not alone. Many students find themselves needing to step back during their time at Laurier, and there are pathways to support every individual situation and help you succeed.
The Dean of Students Office is here to assist students who are struggling to find the right way forward when extenuating circumstances impact their ability to engage in academics.

title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
section: Types of Short-Term Absences > Less Than One Week
text: When you are not well enough to attend class or engage in academics for a few days, in lieu of medical documentation, the Illness Self-Declaration Form can be used to request short-term academic consideration for course work due to medical reasons. title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
section: Types of Short-Term Absences > One to Two Weeks
text:
If you are not able to engage in academics for 1-2 weeks, and you feel as though you will be able to return to your course work, you should talk to your instructors as a first step.
If the circumstances are sensitive in nature and you are not able to share the details of your circumstances, or if you are medically unable to contact your instructors yourself, you can connect with the Dean of Students Office for elevated personal support in navigating your circumstances and notifying your instructors of your absence, on your behalf.

title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
section: Types of Short-Term Absences > More Than Two Weeks
text:
If you are experiencing a disruption because of an injury, surgery, or an ongoing medical situation, and your recovery is anticipated to last more than two weeks' time, it is recommended that you inquire about academic accommodations through Accessible Learning.
Generally speaking, once a student misses more than two weeks of course work, it can be extremely difficulty to catch up, especially if the circumstances are complex or if you are still recovering from a medical condition. In these situations, we recommend students meet with their academic advisor to discuss their academic options.

title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
section: What to Consider Before Taking Time Away from Studies
text:
When you begin your university journey, you may not anticipate needing time away from your studies. However, stepping back can be an opportunity to prioritize your well-being, reassess your goals, and return with renewed focus.
• Life is unpredictable, and taking time off, whether for personal, medical, financial, or academic reasons, can be a valuable step toward long-term success.
• You are not alone in this experience. Each year, many students make the decision to take a break, and for many, it provides the clarity and space needed to move forward with confidence.
• Having the right support system is key. We encourage you to connect with family, friends, and your academic advisor to explore your options.
• Remember to show yourself compassion and trust in your academic journey. A break does not mean falling behind; it means making a thoughtful decision to ensure your future academic success.
• Take a moment to reflect: What truly matters to you? What choices today will matter most five years from now?

title: Managing Unexpected Academic Disruptions
section: Returning to Studies After Taking Time Away
text:
If you are looking to return to studies after taking a temporary leave of absence, there are several resources that are helpful to consider after being away from studies:
• Academic Advising for support related to course selection, program progression, and graduation requirements.
• Accessible Learning to inquire about potential academic accommodations if you are returning from surgery or medical-related leave and have ongoing needs.
• Counselling and Personal Support to help build a support network when facing challenging times and looking to return after personal challenges.
• Financial Coaching if you took some time away from school for financial reasons and you would like personalized assistance in creating a financial plan for your return to studies.
• Student Success Services to freshen up your study skills, writing skills, and more, if you have taken some time away from studies and would like to ensure you are set up for academic success when you are back in class.
Successfully returning to studies after time away is possible with the right tools and support. If you are facing complex challenges or if you need assistance in getting connected to multiple resources, or establishing a plan for support moving forward, the Dean of Students Office is available to help provide individualized support.

title: Academic Petitions and Appeals
text:
There are two categories of petitions to a faculty petitions committee:
• An petition may be filed on the grounds that the normal faculty or university rules, calendar requirements and/or Senate-approved regulations have not been properly or fairly applied to your circumstances.
• You may request relief from a faculty or university rule, calendar requirement and/or Senate-approved regulation because of severe extenuating circumstances, such as medical or compassionate grounds. You cannot petition relief from a course policy.
In both types of petitions, a faculty's petitions committee will review your circumstances and supporting documentation and exercise its discretion to decide whether or not to grant an exception.
If you have questions regarding the petition process, arrange to meet with an academic advisor.
